## Purpose and use

This is the single authoritative backlog for the Paloma's Orrery codebase
(~86k lines, ~100 modules) -- a Python/Plotly/Tkinter 3D solar system
visualization suite with a companion Gallery Studio pipeline and web gallery.
It tracks every open item, deferred decision, known bug, design question, and
new idea across the orrery refactor / Movement track and all active work streams.

**What this ledger is for.**

- *Session start:* Claude searches this file first -- open items, Tony's
  `**Tony:**` comments, and any `**Gap:**` notes -- before proposing work.
  It is the shared memory that survives session boundaries.
- *During a session:* blocks are updated in place as work lands. Status,
  gap, and ref fields change; new items are appended with the next L-handle.
  Nothing is renumbered; nothing is re-embedded from a handoff.
- *Between sessions:* Tony adds `**Tony:**` comments to any block as an
  async message to the next session -- questions, observations, things to
  verify visually. Claude reads them at session start and addresses them
  before building. See "Using and maintaining" below.
- *For the record:* closed items move to section C and stay there. The
  archive is not cleaned; it is the project's institutional memory. A future
  session (or Paloma) can reconstruct what was tried, what failed, and why.

**What this ledger is not.**

It is not a session log (that lives in handoffs and the git history). It is
not a design document (design emerges in conversation and lands in code and
comments). It is not a specification (the render is the spec -- Tony's eyes
are the gate). It is a backlog and a shared context artifact: the thing that
keeps the work from drifting between sessions.

**The round trip: protocol -> ledger -> handoff -> manifest -> code -> repo -> ledger.**

The ledger sits within a larger document stack. From the top down:

- *Protocol (the constitution):* the project instructions document the
  practical philosophy and operating conventions of the Tony-Claude
  partnership -- modes, criticality tiers, anti-patterns, technical
  standards, and the principles behind them. It is the load-bearing
  structure that everything else rests on. It evolves slowly and
  deliberately; amendments are proposed in conversation, ratified by Tony,
  and committed to the repo. Every session starts from it.
- *Ledger -> conversation:* an open item, a Tony comment, or a gap note
  becomes the seed for a design conversation. The conversation produces
  clarity -- options narrow, architecture simplifies, decisions land.
- *Conversation -> handoff:* what was done and what remains gets written
  into a handoff document. Most handoffs are session records: decisions
  made, code delivered, scope of what is still open. A handoff is a claim,
  not a verification -- the render and the repo are the facts. But some
  handoffs have a longer life: orbital mechanics, Gallery/Studio design, and
  similar foundational topics are maintained as durable design documents,
  updated in place as the domain evolves. These are reference artifacts, not
  session logs.
- *Handoff -> manifest (sometimes):* for complex multi-file builds, a
  handoff is distilled into a manifest -- specific, ordered instructions
  for code modifications, file by file, function by function. Not every
  handoff becomes a manifest; small or targeted work goes straight from
  handoff to code without one.
- *Code -> repo:* every change -- code and documentation alike -- is
  committed and pushed to the GitHub repo before the next session begins.
  The repo at HEAD is the source of truth for every turn. The SHA is the
  unforgeable confirmation that commit, push, and sync all landed; a
  matching remote HEAD is the round-trip check. Nothing builds on unverified
  ground.
- *Repo -> ledger:* once work is pushed and render-confirmed, the relevant
  ledger block is updated in place -- status, gap, ref, and any note worth
  keeping. New bugs, new ideas, and deferred observations get their own
  blocks. The ledger absorbs what the session produced and becomes the
  springboard for the next conversation.

The manifests and session-record handoffs are working documents -- they live
their life in a session and then become history. The durable handoffs, the
protocol, and the ledger are the persistent artifacts: they carry forward
what the project still needs to know, each at its own level of abstraction.

**Structure.** DETAIL blocks are the single source of truth. The INDEX below
is generated from them by `ledger_index.py` -- edit a block, re-run the tool.
Handles are append-only (L-###); a closed item keeps its handle
and moves to section C. Section layout:

- **A** -- cross-cutting / strategic items
- **PENDING** -- action items waiting on a specific gate (test, push, decision)
- **D.*** -- open work, organized by type (Movement, Priority, Structural, etc.)
- **E** -- AU-convention compliance cluster (standing convention sweep)
- **G** -- open questions / Tony's calls
- **H** -- Gallery / Studio track
- **C** -- reconciled done items (archive; do not re-do)

This file lives at the repository root alongside `MODULE_ATLAS.md` and
`PROVENANCE_AUDIT.md` as an authoritative generated-index artifact. The git
log carries the SHA history; this file carries the backlog.

## Verification convention (honesty about this ledger's own claims)

A handoff is a claim; the code is closer to fact. Each status carries a tag:

- `[verified @SHA]` -- checked against the live repo code in the named session.
- `[per chain; not re-verified]` -- carried from a handoff's prose; status is
  as the handoff stated, NOT re-confirmed against HEAD this session.
- `[render-gated]` -- correctness is a Mode-5 judgment, not settleable here.
- `[render-confirmed Mode 5]` -- Tony's eyes passed it on live data.

Items with no tag are administrative (tracks, actions) rather than code claims.

---

## ID + status convention

Live-backlog items carry an append-only handle **L-###** (assigned once, never
reused or reordered) so each is greppable for life. A pre-existing number is kept
inline as an alias: `[L-027 | #61]`, `[L-040 | #19]`. Section-C archive items keep
legacy numbers (no retroactive L-###). When an L-### item closes it keeps its
handle and moves to C.

The **DETAIL blocks are the single source of truth.** The INDEX zone is GENERATED
from them by `ledger_index.py` -- edit one block, regenerate; index and detail
cannot desync (module_atlas pattern).

- DISPOSITION (one per item): `DONE | PENDING-GATE | OPEN | BLOCKED | DEFERRED | PARKED | OBSERVED`
- EVIDENCE (separate axis, in the detail): `[verified @SHA] | [render-confirmed Mode 5] | [render-gated] | [per chain]`
- `**Gap:**` states the blocker/next-action on anything not DONE; `**Ref:**` points at the authority (handoff / SHA / code).
- `render-confirmed Mode 5` is EVIDENCE, not a disposition. It means Tony's
  eyes passed the output on live data -- a DONE item can carry it, and an
  OPEN item can carry it on a partial fix. It does not close an item.
- DONE items stay in their section until a housekeeping pass moves them to C.
  The trigger is `**Gap:** none -- move to section C`. Items in C are closed
  for the record; do not re-do them.

## Using and maintaining this ledger

**Author / update protocol.** Claude is the primary author of the ledger's
content: during a session it drafts and updates detail blocks (new items,
status changes, gap/ref notes), normally at the handoff that closes a session
and only when asked. Tony is the integrator and the only writer to the repo --
Claude has read-only GitHub access, so every change is reviewed and committed
by Tony. Updates are made IN PLACE: edit the relevant detail block; do not
re-embed a fresh copy. Handles are append-only -- a new item takes the next
unused L-### (read the highest in use off the index; do not trust a number
written here, which goes stale the moment it is written);
a closed item keeps its L-### and moves to section C.

**ledger_index.py -- what it does, when to run it.** The DETAIL blocks are the
single source of truth; the INDEX tables below are GENERATED from them. After
any edit to a block -- a new item, a status change, an edited title or date --
regenerate the index so the board matches the detail:

    python ledger_index.py LEDGER_CONSOLIDATED.md

Run it from the repo root, where both files live (on Windows it is `python`,
not `python3`). It rewrites only the zone between the INDEX:START / INDEX:END
markers, so it is safe to re-run and never touches your prose. To validate
without rewriting -- catches duplicate handles or a malformed metadata line --
add `--check`:

    python ledger_index.py LEDGER_CONSOLIDATED.md --check

**Finding an item (Windows / VS Code).** Every item is keyed by its L-handle,
so you never scroll. In VS Code, Ctrl+F opens Find in this file -- type an
L-handle (e.g. `L-012`) to land on both its index row AND its detail block;
type a legacy alias (`#61`, `19.3`) to find it by its old number. To LIST
matches rather than jump to them -- e.g. every open item -- use the Search
panel (Ctrl+Shift+F) and search `| ! |` (the gap marker); it shows all hits at
once. PowerShell equivalent, if you prefer the command line:
`Select-String -Path LEDGER_CONSOLIDATED.md -Pattern 'L-012'`.

**Default path (Run button / bare invocation).** `ledger_index.py` now falls
back to `LEDGER_CONSOLIDATED.md` in its own folder when called with no
argument -- so pressing the Run button in VS Code, or typing bare
`python ledger_index.py`, just works. Pass an explicit path to override;
`--check` still works with or without an explicit path.

**Tony's comment convention -- async notes between sessions.** Any DETAIL
block may carry a `**Tony:**` paragraph between the narrative and the
`**Gap:**` line. These are free-form: questions, second-thoughts, design
observations, things to verify visually. The metadata parser ignores them,
so they cannot break the index. At the start of a review session Claude
searches for every `**Tony:**` block and addresses them before building.
Date-stamp is optional but useful: `**Tony (2026-06-17):**`. A `**Note:**`
tag (no date required) works the same way for factual addenda from either
side. For a free-floating thought with no obvious home, either attach it to
the nearest relevant item or open a new `D.LooseEnd` item for it -- floating
notes get lost; capturing on first mention is the rule.

**RICE scoring -- prioritization for planning.** Each DETAIL block's
metadata line can carry an optional `rice:R/I/C/E` field at the end:

    <!-- L:999 status:OPEN upd:2026-06-18 section:D.Movement flag: rice:3/3/100/2 -->

The four dimensions, adapted for this project:

    R (Reach/Value)    Educational or visual value
                       3 = core experience  2 = gallery quality  1 = internal hygiene
    I (Impact)         Magnitude of improvement
                       3 = new capability  2 = meaningful  1 = polish  0.5 = marginal
    C (Confidence %)   Scope clarity
                       100 = ready to build  80 = mostly scoped  50 = needs design  25 = speculative
    E (Effort)         Sessions to complete
                       0.5 = quick fix  1 = one session  2 = two sessions  3 = three+

    Score = R x I x (C / 100) / E

Separator is `/` (not `.`) so decimal values like `0.5` work. Omit the
field entirely or use `rice:-` for unscored items -- both display as `--`
in the INDEX. `ledger_index.py` parses the field, computes the score, and
sorts scored items to the top of their section (descending); unscored
items follow by L-number. Completed items carry their score into section C
as an archive of the prioritization thinking -- no cleanup on close.

#### [L-528] The orrery's Kepler solvers' start: E = pi for a stretched orbit, and no error when they do not converge (orrery; recorded, not built)
<!-- L:528 status:OPEN upd:2026-11-12 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Opened 2026-11-12**, at the close of L-524 (the Kepler solver's
  start), to carry the list that item recorded and did not fix (its
  brief: "list them by file and function, and fix none"). Read at
  orrery 17580bc5 by the L-524 session.
- **Start at E = pi for e of 0.8 or more,** as the gallery's old solver
  did: `apsidal_markers.py` `solve_kepler_equation`;
  `exoplanet_orbits.py` `solve_kepler_equation`; `sgr_a_star_data.py`
  `solve_kepler_equation`; `palomas_orrery.py`, four inline copies
  (`plot_actual_orbits` near line 4610; two workers near 5407 and 5863;
  `animation_worker` near 6990); `test_orbit_markers.py`
  `solve_kepler`. Other starts: `hills_cloud_sampler.py`
  `_eccentric_anomaly` (M + e sin M); `main_belt_sampler.py` `_kepler`
  (M).
- **Why safe today, and when it would not be:** every start-at-pi copy
  is handed M in [0, 2 pi), the side where that start converges; a
  caller handing in a negative M would get a wrong answer. None raises
  when it does not converge.
**Gap:** an orrery session: the gallery's fix (solve for |M| on [0, pi],
start at pi, sign from M, raise when not converged) and a check of the
gallery's "Kepler solver" kind, in the orrery's maintenance run. Between
builds, never in front of the road.
**Ref:** L-524 (the Kepler solver's start, the gallery's fix and its
check `tools/test_kepler_solver.py`); L-525 (hold the bad data).

#### [L-522] Document caps: how the working documents are kept from growing, and the catch-up (protocol, skills, ledger; upkeep)
<!-- L:522 status:OPEN upd:2026-11-11 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **The review, 2026-11-10**
  (`documentation/REVIEW_fundamental_documents_20261110.md`, read at
  orrery b3ce81f8 and gallery cea21af1; the coordinating session, Claude
  Fable 5.2). Tony asked for the governing documents to be reviewed for
  gaps, effectiveness and efficiency. The finding in one sentence: each
  document has a rule for how a line gets in and none for how a line
  leaves, so each carries its own history and only grows. The
  measurements are in the review and are not repeated here.
- **Tony's rulings, 2026-11-10** (quoted with their times in
  `documentation/DESIGN_document_caps_rulings_20261110.md`):
  - Growth is held by a length cap on each working document. 09:48: "I
    used to have a length cap on the project instructions at 800 lines.
    There really no other method to control growth."
  - A session pays where it touches, with a review from time to time.
    09:48: "Generally where I touch works best with periodic
    reassessments like this one. For the master plan generally that's
    when a major build is finished."
  - Upkeep goes between builds, never in front of one. 09:42, on the
    Braid: "builds were being delayed by what I saw as secondary items.
    The idea is to move along themes."
  - The three rules and the six steps below: 09:57, "That makes sense."
    and 10:02, "This makes sense. I would like this session to work as
    the coordinator and we can split off chunks as we decide, on a
    priority basis between other sessions as you said."
  - Step 1 goes before Mars. 12:21: "before. Mars is the next part of
    the braid. you can proceed with step 1."
- **The method, three rules.** (1) Each working document has a cap, in
  lines, and an overflow home: the named place an old line goes when it
  leaves. (2) A session that adds to a document at its cap moves
  something out first, to that home. (3) The maintenance run prints
  every document over its cap, by name; only Tony raises a cap's number.
  No new skill.
- **Where the caps are written: on one page, changed after the tools
  were read.** At the talk rule 1 put each cap in the
  document's own first lines. `doc_index.py` reads only the root's
  documents, a skill has no such line, and a cap written into twelve

#### [L-515] One nested tree in place of isolated rooms (gallery, the room system; design)
<!-- L:515 status:OPEN upd:2026-11-10 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Opened 2026-11-07, 00:17 Chicago**, in the coordinating session
  (Claude Opus 5.5), built on orrery 33c699bb and gallery 3f2ce7fc.
  Tony: "I think we need to rethink the room system before we go
  further. The model we are using is that of isolated room with their
  defined features. A solar system room, a sun room, an earth room, next
  a mars room, etc. the problem is that they are isolated and their
  features cannot be shared. I think what we need is a nested system
  much like the orrery's flat objects list:" -- his tree: Solar system;
  Sun (Sun shells; Comets, by type); Mercury (shells); Venus (shells;
  asteroids); Earth (shells; Moon, with Moon shells; space missions, by
  type; asteroids, by type); Mars (shells; Phobos; Deimos); Asteroid
  belt (belt cloud; named asteroids); ... TNOs; Termination shock;
  Heliopause; ... Gravitational influence.
- **Read at gallery 3f2ce7fc:** every object in
  `data/objects_config.json` already names a `parent`: "sun" for 97, none
  for the Sun, and Earth, Jupiter, Saturn and Pluto for the Moon, Io,
  Titan and Charon. The Solar System room's drawer
  (`rooms.solar-system.drawer.rows`, 113 rows) is already in his order:
  the Sun, the comet groups, Mercury, Venus, the Aten group, Earth, the

- **Method, the coordinator's, for the brief and the skills (not Tony's):**
  - PRECISION. A phone's WebGL holds positions as 32-bit floats, about 7
    digits: about 10 km at 1 AU, about 300 km at Pluto's distance,
    against Pluto's 1,188 km radius (the coordinator's arithmetic, to be
    MEASURED in the build). The fix: before a centred or close view is
    drawn, the page shifts the whole drawing so the body in focus sits at
    the scene's origin, in 64-bit numbers; moving our own drawing is not
    the retired subtraction of two JPL answers.
  - COMPOSING A CHILD into the root ADDS the parent's worked-out position
    to the child's own JPL elements around the parent, which involves no
    cancellation. gallery-assembler 1.3's section "No composition between
    frames" says composition "was tried and retired"; the build amends it
    to say which (subtracting two answers stays retired; adding to a
    child's own answer is the method), in that skill's next version.
  - OFF-ORIGIN FRAMES: Go To, Centre on, +, - and Home frame a box centred
    where the view's middle is, not always the Sun. Go To on a moon from
    the Sun's view puts its planet at the middle, fits the moon's whole
    orbit (Go To fits the whole orbit, L-479) and opens the moon's own
    box (L-514 ruling 4; the Earth room's Moon Go To fix, deferred to the
    Mars session, rides 2b).

#### [L-508] A held body's alarm: loud until a ledger item names it (orrery + gallery, the Horizons check and the night)
<!-- L:508 status:OPEN upd:2026-11-08 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Also for the records skill's next version, carried here 2026-11-08**
  (Tony, in his prompt to the lobby design talk): "once I've installed a
  skill or pasted the protocol, any later change to it must get a new
  version number. On Nov 7 the skill and the protocol each changed twice
  under the same number, and the version check can't catch that." It
  refines One Session, One Bump: one number per session holds only until
  Tony installs or pastes; a change after that is a new number, even in
  the same session. The case: interactive-exhibit 1.35 and protocol
  v3.131, Nov 7, night.
- **RULED, Tony, 2026-11-02, evening,** in the coordinating session
  (Claude Opus 5.5), in his words: "A held body raises an alarm. It is
  loud until a ledger item names it. Once an item exists, the report
  line carries that item's number and is quiet. It clears when the item
  is done, and it goes loud again if the item is done but JPL still
  disagrees. This applies to every held body, not only comets. It is a
  method: write it for ledger-and-session-records' next version, with
  provenance-discipline pointing to it rather than repeating it."
- **What a hold is today** (orrery 0d2d2a0e, `horizons_check.py`,
  L-485): an identity JPL no longer gives as the list does holds the
  body at its last confirmation, with a hold block in its record; the
  run prints "HELD <key> -- since <date>: <cause>" and adds "; HELD
  <key> since <date>" to the verdict line, and is not red. Nothing
  links a hold to a ledger item. No body is held today
  (`data/horizons_confirmations.json` has no hold block). The website
  does not read the hold yet (gallery-cache-builder 1.16, A Body the

#### [L-499] The kinds of session: three, told apart by what each writes, with the build session in two forms (protocol, Mode 7)
<!-- L:499 status:OPEN upd:2026-10-29 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Ruled at the talk of 2026-10-27** (`documentation/DESIGN_talk_20261027_rulings.md`,
  section 7). Claude put four kinds to Tony (coordinating, build,
  talk-only, Code). Tony: "I would included a Code session as a kind
  of builder session. Thoughts?" Agreed, and confirmed by Tony:
  - a COORDINATING session (Claude Fable 5.1, linked to Tony's
    computer) verifies against both repositories at HEAD, runs design
    talks, and writes rulings and briefs into the orrery's
    documentation folder; no patch, no code;
  - a TALK-ONLY session (Opus or Sonnet, not linked) writes design
    records and handoffs in Tony's words, which he saves by hand; no
    patch, no code;
  - a BUILD session writes code, in the PATCH form (Cowork: a patch
    file Tony runs with the Run button, the spent patch the record,
    the test result reaching the session through his run record) or
    the DIRECT form (Claude Code, one repository folder: files edited
    in place, the tests run and read by the session before it closes,
    the change list in GitHub Desktop and the Where We Are box the
    record). In both forms it reads the brief through Where We Are,
    fires the same skills, ends with the records, and leaves commit
    and push to Tony.
- **Two lessons of Oct 27 for the coordinating session's own rules**
  (the record's section 7): a build session in the direct form
  verifies against the files in front of it, one step fresher than
  the repo at HEAD; and a file placed on Tony's computer from the
  coordinating session is confirmed by reading it back, not by the
  tool's answer.
- **The two texts that said four kinds:** the master plan's Section 11
  paragraph (v37), corrected 2026-10-27, evening, in place, with a
  note saying so, and the executive summary's line pointing at it;
  the Oct 26 brief's section 4, which is history and is not edited

- **2026-10-27, evening:** CLAUDE.md gained its "How to report to

- **2026-10-29, the door in the parent folder** (Tony's prompt of Oct 28,

  named, its failure mode written down, and its failure made visible
  rather than silent (L-485's R4). The record's first names: who
  besides Tony can hold the GitHub account and the Google sign-in;
  JPL Horizons' interface; the Plotly library served from an outside
  address; GitHub Pages itself; GitHub's pause of scheduled workflows
  in a repository with no commits for sixty days.
- Discovery first, one list; remediation later, in slices (The Braid).
  Tony's to shape at a talk of its own.
- **Opened 2026-10-26** in the records patch for L-485 and L-489, on
  Tony's answer in chat that it be an item of its own.
- **2026-10-30, the sixty-day pause, read from GitHub** (L-485's
  orrery session). "In a public repository, scheduled workflows are
  automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in
  60 days." (docs.github.com, "Events that trigger workflows" and
  "Disabling and enabling a workflow".) Neither page defines repository
  activity, so whether the nightly commits count is not written down.
  Built: the workflow's last step, every night, clean or red, runs `gh
  workflow enable nightly.yml`. Two facts GitHub does not write down:
  whether enabling a workflow that is already on resets the count; and
  a workflow already paused does not run, so it cannot revive itself.
  The documented way back is on the same page: "if a user with `write`
  permissions to the repository makes a commit that changes the `cron`
  schedule on the workflow, the workflow will be reactivated", or the
  Enable button on the Actions tab. How the failure shows: the
  dashboard's nightly line turns red, "no clean run since", a day
  after the last clean run.
- **2026-10-30, who is told when a scheduled run fails:**
  "Notifications for scheduled workflows are sent to the user who
  initially created the workflow" (docs.github.com, "Notifications for
  workflow runs"); a different user who changes the cron takes them
  over, and after a pause they go to whoever re-enabled the workflow.
  Today that is Tony. A legacy fact: whoever holds the account holds
  the notices.
- **2026-10-31, the website's half** (L-485's gallery session): its
  workflow carries the same keep-alive, `gh workflow enable
  nightly.yml`, `if: always()`, with the same two unwritten facts. Two
  more things the website leans on, now named: GitHub's rate limit on
  unsigned questions, which its runners' shared addresses could spend
  ("Unauthenticated requests are associated with the originating IP
  address"), answered by the pulls asking with the run's own token; and
  GitHub Pages redeploying on the bot's commit, seen in the orrery
  (runs 1175 and 1177) and to be seen for the website itself on its
  first run by hand.
- **Tony, 2026-11-07, 12:35 Chicago, in chat**, after the coordinator
  named a long run of red nights as the risk no schedule covers: "Only
  Claude can back me up as. I have 250$". Proposed by the coordinator
  the same hour (L-485's Note): a Claude caretaker, a scheduled task on
  Tony's account that reads the nightly runs on GitHub (this cloud
  cannot reach JPL, so GitHub's run keeps the fetching), switches a
  paused schedule back on, and, after a red night, makes only repairs of
  named kinds that keep the site drawing, each written to the ledger
  and Where We Are and reported to Tony, anything else written up and
  left; each run reports its token count. Named limit: the caretaker
  runs on Tony's account and payment, so the accounts themselves are
  still the part it cannot hold.
- **Tony's ruling, 2026-11-07, 12:43 Chicago, in chat:** "Yes. And token
  conservation should be a key objective. My GitHub account is free but
  Claude is not." The caretaker may commit a short list of repairs Tony
  approves, the first exception to "commit and push are Tony's"; the
  list comes to him before anything is set up; each run spends the
  fewest tokens that do its job and reports its count.
- **His question, the same message:** "If my subscription is suspended
  what happens with my cloud credit and caretaker schedule? Bottom line:
  what would happen to Palomas Orrery once I'm "gone"." Answered from
  what could be read on 2026-11-07: the caretaker runs on his Claude
  account and stops with it; what becomes of remaining credit was not
  readable (support.claude.com's "Using extra usage" page did not load)

  determine what happens to the account's content", and a designated
  successor is one who can ask; "Maintaining ownership continuity of

#### [L-489] Compositions: a curated view within a room, authored in the editor (gallery, the rooms)
<!-- L:489 status:OPEN upd:2026-10-28 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Opened 2026-10-26** from the design talk of Oct 25, evening
  (`documentation/DESIGN_compositions_rulings_20261025.md`, Claude
  Fable 5.1's record, zero code). Prompted by build B's finding that
  drawing the Sun's far shells with Voyager's path breaks the Solar
  System room's rule that a body's shells live in its own room (L-488).
- **Tony, in the talk:** "The difference is that the objects list in
  the orrery is basically flat. We can combine any object and feature.
  In the website the room structure is not flat. Thoughts?" Then:
  "What's new here is the curatorial element. Up to now it's all
  general rules for all rooms. Specific curatorial decisions by room is
  a new approach. Perhaps this could be part of gallery editor." His two
  examples: "solar system room, spacecraft, voyager 1 room: object +
  sun, earth, mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, Pluto." And: "sun
  room, major planets + Pluto, voyager 1 and 2 room: earth, mars,
  Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Pluto, f corona, Alfven surface, termination
  shock, heliopause."
- **Tony's rulings, Oct 25:**
  - C1, the shape, put to him and confirmed ("Yes"): a composition is a
    named selection from what its host room can draw, authored in the
    editor, served as data, with its own address.
  - C2, an interpretation. Tony: "and a way to explain what it shows,
    an interpretation. Maybe in the info panel." Each composition
    carries words saying what the view shows and why it matters, in the
    i panel, beside the sources that back it.
  - C3, a spacecraft is a story. Tony: "spacecraft are not just
    missions they are stories, why there were made, what they find,
    etc. they weave together the astronomy and the human exploration.
    And yes we can source that story from nasa, esa, etc." The story is
    sourced, not recalled, under the provenance rules already in force:
    a claim about what a mission found is cited to the agency's page; an
    agency summary that names no source is a lead, read one layer down
    (Tony's ruling of Oct 21); a number in it is a served number; a
    claim that cannot be sourced is left out with the gap noted.
- **The principle, from the record:** the orrery is flat because its
  user is its author; the website is not, because its user is a visitor
  on a phone, and the rooms are the curation. General rules for every
  room stay method, in the skills; compositions are curation, Tony's,
  and are data.
- **Claude's reading in the record, for the design talk, not ruled:**
  a composition is a served list (its host room, the keys it ticks, the
  frame it opens on, a title, the interpretation), read as the arrival
  block is read, with no room built in code for it. The exhibit store
  editor (`tools/exhibit_store_editor.py`, writing through
  `tools/store_writer.py`) gains a section that writes it, under the
  same checks as the served words, plus a cache check that it names
  only keys the cache serves. A composition picks only from what its
  host room can draw: example 1 costs almost nothing once slice 2 is
  live; example 2 needs the Sun room to draw planets and paths, which
  is a build. "Room" stays the code-level thing; a composition gets its
  own noun and its own address. The room rule is restated, not broken:
  a shell may be listed in several compositions and is stored once.
- **Under this item:**
  - L-486 (a view carried into a room): largely answered, by the
    record's reading: a composition is a carried view the author
    composed once, on purpose.
  - L-488 (the heliopause beside a spacecraft): Voyager at the
    heliopause is the first composition that needs the Sun's far shells
    in the Solar System room, or the planets and paths in the Sun room;
    which host is Tony's curatorial call, with the discovery list in
    hand.
  - L-483 (a comet room) would become, by the record's reading, the
    second composition, hosted in the Solar System room once it draws
    the comet and its pieces. Not ruled; L-483 keeps its own Gap.
- **Sequence, from the record:** after slice 2 (L-443). Discovery first
  (The Braid): one list of what each room can draw today against what
  the first few compositions need, so the gap is countable before
  anything is built. Then the editor's section and the served shape,
  with example 1 first; then the Sun room's growth, if example 2 still
  wants it.
- **2026-10-27, the talk** (`documentation/DESIGN_talk_20261027_rulings.md`, section 3).
  Tony: "Yes I agree. But let's complete the sun and earth slices
  first. Then we can work on compositions. And we should consider at
  that time whether encounters come first or as compositions."
  - Compositions wait until the Sun's slice (L-412) and Earth's list
    (L-413) are complete.
  - When they are picked up, the first question is whether encounters
    (road stage 12) come first on their own or as scenes.
  - The noun is "scene": Tony's "Yes I agree" to the recommendation,
    told it would be recorded so, with no objection. "View" already

    `?exhibit=solar-system&scene=voyager-1`.
  - The first scene stays example 1, Voyager 1 with its planets in
    the Solar System room, unless he says otherwise then.
- **Received 2026-10-28 from L-501 (2026 ED138), at its close:** the
  exhibit store editor should offer a new body's two edits as a form:

- **Received 2026-11-09, night, from L-519 at its close** (Featured's

#### [L-486] A view carried into a room (gallery, the rooms)
<!-- L:486 status:OPEN upd:2026-10-26 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Tony, 2026-10-24, night,** in his run record (`documentation/WHERE_WE_ARE_10-24-26_1927_run_record.md`):
  "an idea for consideration. in the orrery, the sun features can be
  combined with other objects, like say the earth's orbit. in the
  website we start in the solar system room, but if we then enter the
  sun room, or the earth room, those views are completely reset. this
  would also apply to any other sub-rooms, other planets, satellites,
  encounters, comet breakups, etc. What i am wondering is if we could
  enable a way to retain a view we create before entering a room and
  keep it." His examples: the inner planets' orbits kept when the Sun
  room's dust cloud is added; a comet carried into its own room, with
  its perihelion and its Roche limit. "specific encounter events could
  be duplicated of course, like perihelion events in the sun room, or
  close encounter asteroids in the earth room. or spacecraft flybys. so
  for many events, these duplicates would do the job. the exception
  would be sun features without sun encounters."
- **Claude, the same night:** the hard part is that each room draws at
  its own scale and around its own centre. The Sun room works in solar
  radii, the inner planets' orbits are about 200 times wider, and the
  Earth room is centred on Earth. Carrying a selection means a room
  learns to draw the other room's objects at its scale. The duplicated
  events Tony names are things a room already knows how to draw.
- **2026-10-26: under L-489 (compositions),** opened from the design
  talk of Oct 25, evening
  (`documentation/DESIGN_compositions_rulings_20261025.md`). That
  record's reading: this item is largely answered by a composition, a
  view the author composed once, on purpose, instead of one a visitor
  carries in at the wrong scale.

at its design talk; this item closes with it, or keeps whatever a
composition does not answer.

#### [L-485] A nightly unattended run of the routines (orrery + gallery, maintenance)
<!-- L:485 status:OPEN upd:2026-11-10 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Tony, 2026-10-24, night,** in his run record (`documentation/WHERE_WE_ARE_10-24-26_1927_run_record.md`): "i am
  thinking of revising the idea of an automated run at midnight every
  day, with all the daily and 30-day run routines except the messages.
  i would still have to look at these daily, unless the autorun just
  reports any new messages and continues. now with the rerun fix this
  should work. the question is whether this would require my machine
  to be on all night. not impossible."
- **Claude, the same night:** Windows' Task Scheduler can wake a
  sleeping computer to run a task, though not one that is shut down.
  Since patch_L443_10 the path plan saves as it goes and keeps under
  the maintenance run's 15 minutes, so it cannot hang such a run. The
  line to hold: the run fetches, generates and checks unattended;
  committing and pushing stay Tony's, from a short report in the
  morning.
- **Corrected 2026-10-26:** the note above is overturned twice by
  Tony's rulings of Oct 25. The checkers, not Tony, gate the nightly
  push (R1, below), and no machine of his wakes: the run is on GitHub's
  computers (R3). The note is kept as the record of the first idea.
- **The design talk, 2026-10-25**
  (`documentation/DESIGN_L485_nightly_run_rulings_20261025.md`, Claude
  Fable 5.1's record, zero code). The purpose, Tony at 13:11: "There are
  really only two reasons for automation: keeping a cadence of midnight
  runs and fully automated in the event I cannot work the website. So I
  would want to move the 30 day checks to the automated run not just
  the maintenance run. This website is a legacy gift for Paloma."
  Earlier in the talk, on a run that would still need his push each
  morning: "Well if I'm pushing anyway there's really no gain."
- **Tony's rulings, Oct 25:**
  - R1, the checkers are the gate for the nightly push. Tony: "I think
    we have enough safeguards." Put to him and confirmed by his going on
    to the next question: the push happens only on a clean run (every
    gating checker passes and the cache swap succeeded; one red line
    and nothing is committed, and the previous cache stays live); the
    nightly commit touches only what the tools write (the served cache
    under `data/solar-system/`, the run records, the swap log, the
    pulled export and its mirror, the guest book file; in the orrery,
    the data files its 30-day tools write), never code, a page or a word
    a visitor reads, and a run that would change anything else fails
    instead of committing; a failed night is visible, in a dated log and
    the dashboard's last-run line.
  - R2, the 30-day checks move inside the automation: the Horizons
    check, the period fetch, the path plan's re-check, the link check.
    Otherwise the website's own gate, Horizons confirmations within 30
    days, would stop every push a month after Tony's last orrery run.
  - R3, it runs on GitHub's computers (GitHub Actions), not Tony's.
    Tony: "Yes on running on GitHub." The plan to wake a sleeping
    machine is not built.
  - R4, outside failure points are reported, never halting. Tony: "the
    other failure points are beyond our control and should be reported
    but not halt the rest of the run or future runs." The guest book's
    Google sign-in expiring, JPL changing its interface or being down, a
    source address no longer answering, an outside library's address
    failing: each is logged, and the rest of the run and the next
    night's go on.
  - R5, the guest book step reports and continues: the run lists the
    form's new messages in the log; approving, replying and pinning stay
    Tony's. From his note of Oct 24, above: "unless the autorun just
    reports any new messages and continues."
- **Proposed by Claude in the talk, not ruled:**
  - P1, awaiting Tony's word at the build's design talk: when a 30-day
    check disagrees (a Horizons DISAGREES, a comet with a newer record,
    a period JPL now gives differently), that body keeps its last
    confirmed values, whose fetched date the hover and the i panel
    already print, and the disagreement is logged where a reader finds
    it. The automation never decides one.
  - P2, the orrery tools that run at night: period_fetch.py,
    horizons_check.py, path_plan.py, export_objects.py,
    export_constants.py, export_drawings.py and the link check. Not the
    parts of the maintenance run that judge code: the provenance scanner
    as a gate, the constants change report, the reset-completeness test.
  - P3, two workflows, one per repository: the orrery's first, the
    website's about an hour later, each pushing only to its own
    repository with GitHub's built-in token, so no cross-repository
    credential exists to renew; scheduled off the hour (for example
    23:17 and 00:47 UTC).
  - P4, the run pushes from night one, and Tony reads its log each
    morning for the first week.
- **Before the design is trusted, the build session verifies** (the
  record's section 4): whether the nightly commits count as activity
  against GitHub's pause of scheduled workflows in a repository with no
  commits for sixty days (if not, a keep-alive, recorded on L-490); the
  runners' tools (Python with the orrery's libraries, node and a
  headless Chromium) and each job's time against GitHub's limits, the
  path plan's full re-check having run 28 minutes on Tony's machine on
  Oct 24; that the built-in token may push and GitHub Pages redeploys on
  the workflow's commit; that the orrery's tools write LF and ASCII on
  Linux and assume no Windows paths; how the guest book's Google sign-in
  is stored for a runner, and that its expiry fails soft (R4).
- The method the record names goes to gallery-cache-builder at its next
  version. L-462 (a shorter run) is reconsidered in this light, on its
  own block. The record's legacy item is L-490.
- **2026-10-27, P1 ruled** (`documentation/DESIGN_talk_20261027_rulings.md`, section 1).
  Put to Tony as three ways to treat a body whose 30-day check now

  changed is ASCII. A red night writes nothing and names every reason

  `data/nightly_run_record.json`: its UTC stamp (utc_clock), each row's
  verdict, each skipped row and why, and the address of the run's log
  on GitHub. So the committed copy is always the last clean run's.

  after the pulls, `daily_run.py` compares each pull's recorded orrery
  commit (the three .sha files) with the newest commit in the orrery

  stops the run before the builder, naming both commits, the two likely
  causes and what to do; a folder it cannot read stops it too. `--check`

  gallery-cache-builder 1.12.
- **2026-10-30, a second honest cause** (L-485's orrery half). Once the
  orrery's nightly run commits on GitHub, Tony's orrery folder is behind
  GitHub every morning until he clicks Pull origin. The Daily Run's
  check reads that folder, so a difference can now mean "not yet

#### [L-459] A monthly run for slow checks, started by the Daily Run (gallery + orrery, maintenance)
<!-- L:459 status:OPEN upd:2026-10-30 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Tony, 2026-10-20**, in a design chat on verification: "add a monthly

  monthly run rather than a 30-day counter in each check, "Yes, as

- **Started by the Daily Run, never remembered** (A Check That Cannot
  Fail Is Not Passing: put the check where it runs). The run keeps the
  date of its last run in a file. Each Daily Run reads it and starts the
  monthly run once 30 days or more have passed, so a missed day or a
  month away still fires on the next run. On other days it prints one
  line: when the monthly run last ran and when it is next due, so a
  monthly run that stopped happening shows as an old date.
- **Also run by hand, any time** (Tony: "Can I run the checker at
  another time optionally?"): a dashboard button, "Monthly Run -- now",
  runs everything in it at once and resets the date. Tony asked for the
  30-day checks on the dashboard; the Horizons Check's "everything,
  now" button was added the same evening (L-266).

- **The Horizons Check is not moved into it.** It already keeps its own

#### [L-425] A citation's location record is checked only in part (provenance tooling)
<!-- L:425 status:OPEN upd:2026-10-09 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Measured 2026-10-08** at orrery e5cc4bb2, for Tony's question: "how
  do we ensure that a citation's location record is correct and not
  broken or missing. is this check included in the scanner?" The answer
  is no: the scanner checks that a citation sits near a number, not
  where it points. The full table is section B of
  `documentation/TESTING_PROTOCOL_provenance_skills_20261008.md`.
- What is checked: a missing Source line (scanner, Tier-1, gates the
  push); a V_SOURCED row with no Source line (test_status_lines.py,
  gates); a worksheet named in a Cross-checked line and missing
  (worksheet_checker.py layer L0, report-only).
- **Corrected 2026-10-09, by the planted-fault run below:** in
  constants_new.py the scanner does NOT catch a removed Source line
  when the row above is cited within its 30-line look-back (F1), and
  the L0 finding is named only in WORKSHEET_CHECK.md, never in the
  maintenance run's summary line (F4).
- What is not: a missing Access line (20 of 61 sourced or cross-checked
  rows in constants_new.py have none, among them KM_PER_AU and
  SUN_RADIUS_KM); a missing Read line (4 of 61); a record file named on
  a Read line and missing (17 named, all present today); a web address
  that no longer opens (40 distinct addresses, never tested); and
  whether the page says the number, which no tool can check.
- **Three levels proposed, cheapest first:** (1) every file a citation
  names exists, failing the run; (2) every sourced row carries an Access
  line with an address and a date, reported by name first and failing
  only after Tony rules which rows are excused; (3) a link check that
  visits each address, run on Tony's machine, report-only. (1) and (2)
  would be rules in test_status_lines.py, which the maintenance run
  already has.
- **2026-10-09, the planted-fault run** (record: `documentation/HANDOFF_L418_testing_20261009.md`, Part 2, with
  every checker's line word for word). Throwaway clone of orrery
  1e30953; a baseline run first; each fault on its own served row.
  - F1, `# Source:` removed from EARTH_THERMOPAUSE_ALTITUDE_KM
    (V_SOURCED): caught by test_status_lines.py alone, which gates. The
    scanner was silent: the stratopause row's citation, within its
    look-back, was credited to it (removing that too gave 296 to 298).
    On L-414.
  - F2, `# Access:` removed from TERMINATION_SHOCK_AU: silent.
  - F3, HELMET_CUSP_LOW_RADII's record file renamed to a missing one:
    silent, and the broken path is copied into constants_export.json.
  - F4, EARTH_POLAR_RADIUS_KM's worksheet renamed to a missing one:

    line stayed "74 of 110 routed, 8 clean".
  - F5, EARTH_VAN_ALLEN_OUTER_BAND_LOW_L's address changed to a missing

  - F6, EARTH_MAGNETOPAUSE_SHUE_A1_RADII's Read moved from Table 1 to

    test_constants_export.py fail, all gating; the worksheet checker

  - F7b, GRAVITATIONAL_CONSTANT_SI's value moved alone (not served; its

#### [L-426] The worksheet checker compares very small numbers as equal (worksheet checker)
<!-- L:426 status:OPEN upd:2026-10-09 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Found 2026-10-09** by the planted-fault run (F7b; record `documentation/HANDOFF_L418_testing_20261009.md`).
  `compare()` in `worksheet_checker.py` rounds the code's value and the
  worksheet's to the coarser of their DECIMAL PLACES. For numbers near
  1e-11 both round to 0, so any two of them match. Probe at 1e30953:
  1e-11, 9.9e-11, 6.674e-11 and 2e-7 each "MATCH" 6.67430e-11, while
  7.0e-5 against 7.292115e-5 is still a MISMATCH. Both drift (L2b) and
  agreement (L2a) use `compare()`, so a moved value on such a row is
  invisible. The one row it reaches today is GRAVITATIONAL_CONSTANT_SI,
  the only constants row this session found whose worksheets give a
  value verdict of YES.
- The rounding is on purpose -- 243 in the code must match 243.0226 in a
  worksheet -- so the fix is to round to significant figures rather than
  to decimal places, not to drop the rounding. Method, not Tony's: he
  asked on 2026-10-09 whether to compare at full digits, and this was
  the answer.
- A change to a checker gets its own session (Where We Are, Settled,
  2026-10-08). L-424's session opens the same function; carry both,
  with a test that fails on the probe values first.
**Gap:** the fix and its test; then the probe values report MISMATCH
and 6.67430e-11 still matches 6.6743e-11.
**Ref:** `worksheet_checker.py` (`compare`, `displayed_precision`,
`float_precision`); `test_worksheet_checker.py`; L-424; L-425.

    position". The last word was "for this body" as offered; changed

    2030, so "none for this body" would be false for them.
  - **The surface line, an old ruling restored.** Build 1 had dropped
    it for the Sun, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune and Planet 9, on
    the three reviewers' proposal ("only where the centre has a solid
    surface"), which the design record left for this look. Tony:
    "previously we measured from 1 radius", and "we decided 'surface'
    meant the solid surface or the gas surface as defined as one
    radius" -- decided "more than a year ago before the ledger
    started". Restored for every centre with a radius in
    `CENTER_BODY_RADII`, worded as before; the checker plants its loss
    and catches it ("SURFACE LINE DROPPED").
  - **What one radius is, for a body without a solid surface**
    (confirmed as recommended): a giant planet's radius is measured to
    the level where the pressure is 1 bar; IAU 2015 Resolution B3: its
    nominal Jupiter radii "correspond respectively to the one-bar
    equatorial and polar radii of Jupiter". The Sun's is the
    photosphere, where the gas turns opaque: the same resolution, its
    nominal solar radius "corresponds to the solar photospheric radius"
    (arXiv:1510.07674, read 2026-10-12, Claude Opus 5.5). Saturn's,
    Uranus's and Neptune's rows cite Archinal et al. 2018; that the
    report states 1 bar itself is NOT yet confirmed. The units, kept
    apart (Tony asked for 1 atm): 1 bar = 100,000 Pa exactly; 1 atm
    (one standard atmosphere) = 101,325 Pa exactly, CGPM 1954
    Resolution 4 (via Wikipedia, "Standard atmosphere (unit)", read
    2026-10-12); 1 atm is about 1.3% more than 1 bar. The convention
    is 1 bar. The orrery's own shell texts for Saturn, Uranus and
    Neptune already say 1 bar.
  - **The lesson, for the record:** a decision older than the ledger
    lives only in what the code does. When a build would remove
    something the orrery already does, it treats that as an old
    decision and asks first.

#### [L-375] Earth's eccentric dipole offset is not drawn (store, Earth)
<!-- L:375 status:OPEN upd:2026-10-22 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Found 2026-09-24** building L-322 D5. Earth's magnetic dipole sits
  off the planet's centre. A source to start from: Koochak and
  Fraser-Smith (2017), Earth and Space Science 4, 626,
  doi:10.1002/2017EA000280; or IGRF-13's degree-2 coefficients with a
  sourced formula. The publisher's site refused the session as a bot, so
  nothing has been read yet.
- Drawing it also needs Earth's rotation phase, which the orrery does
  not model.
- **2026-10-04, re-homed from L-234 at its close:** the website does
  not draw the dipole cone at all; the orrery does, as the swept
  envelope of every azimuth. No ruling against drawing it on the
  website was found. Same question as the offset: what to show when
  the instant depends on a rotation phase neither instrument models.
  Earth's list, design talks (L-413).
- **2026-10-20, design talks** (talk 6 (b); record `documentation/DESIGN_talks_rulings_20261020.md`): the
  offset ruled, Tony: "A". Said in the dipole's hover, not drawn: the
  field's centre sits about N km from Earth's centre, turning with
  Earth. N is worked out from IGRF-14's 2025.0 coefficients (the first
  eight, degrees 1 and 2) by Laundal, K. M. and Richmond, A. D. (2017),
  "Magnetic Coordinate Systems", Space Science Reviews,

#### [L-364] A comet's own trust window can exclude today while the served window passes the scene (gallery, trust)
<!-- L:364 status:OPEN upd:2026-09-29 section:A flag: rice: -->
- **Found 2026-09-26** building L-363, at gallery `a5c35f5f`. Each
  heliocentric object's trust record carries its own window, centred on
  its element epoch. Halley's (anchored at its 1986 perihelion, capped
  at half its period) ends JD 2460350.6, February 2024. Encke's ends JD
  2460843.5, June 2025. Both exclude today.
- The cache's global `served_window` is built in
  `tools/gallery_cache_builder.py` from the SHORTEST window's LENGTH
  (`window_days`, Apophis's today), centred on the build time. It does
  not look at where each object's window falls, and `resolver.py`
  checks a scene's date only against that global window. So a scene of
  today with a comet in it passes, and draws a position the comet's own
  trust record does not vouch for: a check that passes while blind.
- Nothing served draws a comet today. L-363 left both out for this
  reason.
- Tony, 2026-09-26: the trust window will need changes once the
  encounter work starts; not today.
- **2026-09-29:** part of the Solar System room's future under the
  front-door design: each comet apparition becomes a room that opens on
  its perihelion, so this check becomes per apparition (L-393).
**Gap:** The scene date checked against each drawn object's own window, or a served window built from where the windows fall; taken up with the encounter work.
**Ref:** gallery `tools/gallery_cache_builder.py` (served_window, M2 section 5.5); gallery `gallery/assembler/resolver.py`, step 3; skills/gallery-assembler/SKILL.md; L-363.

#### [L-340] The exhibit store editor: what the first screenshot showed, and the Mode 5 pass
<!-- L:340 status:OPEN upd:2026-09-22 section:A flag: rice:3/3/90/1 -->
- **Opened 2026-09-19 because L-334 closed.** The editor is built,
  pushed and working; these are the things left, and a pointer in a
  closed item is not a home for them.
- **THREE THINGS VISIBLE IN TONY'S FIRST SCREENSHOT**, measured at
  gallery `d9d7a48f`, none of which he had hit yet:
  (1) Three shell names are cut off in the left list -- Streamer Belt

  26-character listbox.
  (2) The `source` field is a single-line box 54 characters wide, and
  the Sun core's citation is 134 characters, so about a third of it is
  readable. A citation is a sentence; it wants a wrapped box like
  `description` and `about`.
  (3) The Sun's room shows a Moon tick. Its arrival block carries a
  `moon` key, so the panel offers it, but the Sun's scene has no Moon
  trace -- ticking it writes `true` and changes nothing.
- **A SKILL DESCRIPTION IS CAPPED AT 1024 CHARACTERS**, learned
  2026-09-19 by the upload refusing: "field 'description' in SKILL.md
  must be at most 1024 characters". interactive-exhibit 1.4 came out at
  1042 and would not install; the 35 kB body was never the problem, and
  gallery-cache-builder at 788 went in fine. Every other skill sits
  between 550 and 813, so this is the first time the ceiling has been
  met. Trimmed to 991 in
  `patch_L334_10_skill_description_and_history_20260919.py`.
  **Claude proposes, unratified:** `skills_index.py` should FAIL a run
  whose SKILL.md description exceeds 1024. It already reads every one of
  them to build the manifest, so it is the place where the check would
  actually run rather than be remembered -- and the failure it catches
  is a skill that cannot be installed, which is invisible until someone
  tries and is easy to abandon halfway.
- **ALL THREE ARE FIXED**, by `patch_L340_1_editor_polish_20260919.py`
  at gallery `2ebd001f`, and two of the three were bigger than the
  screenshot suggested. The shell list now sizes itself to the room it is
  showing, between 24 and 58 characters: the longest Earth label is 54,
  "Exosphere / Geocorona (hydrogen halo, detected extent)", not the 36
  the Sun's room showed. The `source` field is a wrapped box like
  `description` and `about`, because the longest served citation is 489
  characters against a 54-character line. And the Sun's arrival block
  lost its `moon` key, while the window now draws the tick only where the
  key exists -- so it can never again offer a control with nowhere to
  save it. [verified @ gallery `2ebd001f`]
- **THAT PATCH WROTE `data/objects_config.json` DIRECTLY, AND THAT IS AN
  EXCEPTION WORTH NAMING.** interactive-exhibit 1.4 says two tools write
  that file: the mirror writes the numbers from the orrery's export, the
  store writer writes the words and the arrival settings. Neither can do
  this one. The writer replaces a value and cannot REMOVE a key, and it
  should not learn how for a single correction. So a one-off correction
  patch wrote the file and named itself the exception in its own
  description. **Owed to interactive-exhibit's next bump:** a one-off
  correction patch may write the file where the writer cannot express the
  change, and it says so in its own description.
  **Tony-action (decide):** whether that exception stays narrow in those
  words. Claude Fable 5.1's view, 2026-09-19, is that it should -- a
  deletion is rare enough that teaching the writer to delete buys less
  than the new ways it could go wrong.
- **THE EXCEPTION WAS USED A SECOND TIME, 2026-09-20, by L-342's
  figures patch.** It added eight served entries to
  `data/objects_config.json` -- an `altitude` or a `radius_km` inside a
  shell's own block, each with its value, unit, figure count and its
  own `orrery_constant`. The mirror cannot CREATE a slot, only fill one

#### [L-337] A centre marker for bodies without shells in the exhibit rooms
<!-- L:337 status:OPEN upd:2026-09-19 section:A flag: rice:3/2/60/2 -->
- **Tony, 2026-09-17, at the phone check of both rooms:** the Sun's room
  has a "Sun" object at the centre, as the orrery does, and Earth's room
  has none; "that might be a useful object to add for future solar system
  scenes without shells."
- **Recorded, not built.** L-334's build contract puts it out of scope
  for that build (its section 7).
- **Tony added to this on 2026-09-19,** and his words settle what the
  marker IS. Quoted as he typed them;
  `documentation/HANDOFF_L334_editor_built_20260919.md` asked the next
  ledger patch to carry this and transcribes the inner quotes as single:

      while it is not a shell or a tick, the "sun" object is useful for
      centering the scene nominally. the earth should have one too in
      case we wish to display no shells. this is an option in the
      orrery.

  And, confirming it the same day for this record, where the orrery
  already draws one:

      the orrery has this too. each object has a symbol, a circle for
      the sun and planets, without any dimension whether or not it has
      any shells. most objects have no drawn shells.

  So the marker is a CENTRING object: a symbol at the body's position
  carrying no dimension, drawn whether or not the body has shells, and
  most objects have none. It is not a shell and it is not a drawer tick.
  The orrery's own per-object symbol is the worked example, which is
  where to look for the shape of the answer.
- **What a build would have to settle first.** What the marker IS is
  ANSWERED as of 2026-09-19, by Tony above: a dimensionless centring
  symbol, not a shell. (Until his answer this bullet read "the Sun's
  centre object may already be that thing, or may be a shell like any
  other, and nobody has looked" -- kept here so the correction is
  visible rather than silent.) STILL OPEN: where it comes from -- drawn
  by the renderer from the served record, or a served feature in its own
  right. And what it says on hover, under the exhibit's provenance
  contract, since a marker at the centre of a body is a natural place to
  put the body's own numbers and those numbers have to be served with
  their source.
- **Claude:** RICE 3/2/60/2 -> 1.8 proposed, unratified. Reach 3 because
  it is every future room rather than only Earth's; Impact 2 because a
  room without it is complete, not broken; Confidence 60 because nothing
  above was settled when it was scored; Effort 2. Tony's answer of
  2026-09-19 settles what the marker is, which argues Confidence up; the
  score is unratified either way.

#### [L-078] Provenance scanner: systematic coverage via module_atlas role classification
<!-- L:078 status:OPEN upd:2026-07-16 section:A flag: rice:2/2/70/3 -->
- **Root cause (why files get missed in the first place).** provenance_scanner.py
  gates display-string scanning on a hand-maintained narrative_files allow-list;
  a new file is invisible until someone notices and adds its name. The scanner
  already solved this once, structurally, for one family -- is_shell_file =
  module_name.endswith('_visualization_shells') auto-includes by pattern, no
  list-editing required -- but that fix was never generalized.
- **module_atlas.py already does most of what's needed and is more complete than
  the scanner's own list.** classify_role() tags every module (data / scenario /
  rendering / rendering-shells / cache / computation / gui / pipeline / utility /
  devtool / legacy / other), with 'other' as an honest catch-all rather than a
  silent drop. Its 'data' role already includes 5 catalog/constants files NOT in
  narrative_files (exoplanet_coordinates, star_properties, stellar_data_patches,
  stellar_parameters, messier_catalog); its 'scenario' role already cleanly
  groups the heat/coral/western family the scanner has no equivalent for. The two
  tools have drifted apart from each other despite Tony running them together --
  nothing actually diffs their outputs. (Minor, telling: food_insecurity_generator
  -- the one file properly in narrative_files -- isn't in module_atlas's ROLE_MAP
  either, so it currently shows 'other' there. Both lists are hand-maintained;
  both have independently drifted.)
- **Design, two checks, both surfacing in PROVENANCE_AUDIT.md (Tony's call --
  that's the output actually reviewed every run, not module_atlas's):**
  1. MISSING CATEGORIES (file-level). Replace/extend narrative_files with
     role-driven inclusion: any module classified data / scenario / rendering /
     rendering-shells gets scanned automatically via module_atlas.classify_role.
     Any module landing in 'other' that contains claim-shaped string content
     gets a new "COVERAGE GAPS -- needs role classification" section in the
     audit output. Mechanical, low risk, the more tractable of the two builds.
  2. MISSING FIELDS (vocabulary-level). Found the exact hook point:
     _extract_string_units (provenance_scanner.py ~L711-721) walks every AST
     string Constant, runs extract_numeric_claims(), and on zero claims just
     `continue`s -- the string vanishes with no trace. Fix: a second, looser
     pattern at that exact branch -- number directly followed by 1-4 letters/%/$
     not matched by NUMERIC_CLAIM_RE -- logged as a near-miss instead of dropped,
     in a new "VOCABULARY GAPS -- unrecognized unit candidates" section. Runs
     only on already-covered files (check 1 handles files missing entirely), so
     naturally narrower scope than a whole-file sweep.
  3. The F/C bare-degree gap itself (KNOWN now, not a near-miss) lands directly
     in NUMERIC_CLAIM_RE as its own fix, separate from the near-miss MECHANISM
     being built to catch the next unknown gap.
- **Noise risk on the near-miss check (the harder of the two, flagged not
  solved).** A loose number+token pattern will catch ordinals ("2nd"), version
  strings ("v3.29"), multipliers ("3x") as false near-misses unless explicitly
  excluded. Needs scratch-testing against the real corpus and an eyeballed
  false-positive rate before going live -- not a guess-and-ship.
- **Architecture: scanner imports classify_role from module_atlas.py directly**
  (Tony: no strong preference, deferred to whatever reliably catches gaps every
  run). One-directional, no third shared module. Default unless revisited.
- **Effort framing (Tony's explicit precedent, 2026-06-30): the original scanner
  took ~10 sessions with multiple Gemini cross-checks to harden.** Not treating
  this as a quick patch. Check 1 (categories) is the tractable mechanical build.
  Check 2 (vocabulary near-miss) is the one likely to need the same kind of
  cross-check / corpus-tuning the original scanner got.
- **STATUS (July 4, 2026): step (1) is LIVE -- role-driven inclusion landed.**
  The scanner at HEAD imports classify_role from module_atlas and uses
  NARRATIVE_ROLES = {data, scenario, rendering, rendering/shells, computation}
  additively over the legacy narrative_files allow-list (line 635-639). The
  COVERAGE GAPS section is working (4 modules flagged: shell_configs 91,
  food_insecurity_generator 1, orrery_rendering 1, smoke_rotation_axis 1).
- **First full run under new coverage: Tier-1 = 104** (all score 16: V=4
  recalled x C=4 public-facing display strings) across 26 modules. Largest
  contributors: idealized_orbits.py (23 findings), paleoclimate_wet_bulb_full

  scenarios_western_heatwave_march_2026 (4), sgr_a_visualization_core (4),
